bias

/BY-uhs/ - rhymes with pious · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bias means a tendency or inclination, conscious or not.

Grandpa owns his bias cheerfully: no tomato from any store will ever beat one from his own garden.

Worked Example

Coach Ruiz never saw her own bias until an assistant charted it: seniors were getting twice the scrimmage minutes of sophomores with equal stats. No rule required it; she had simply leaned, season after season, toward the players she knew longest.

Broader and often gentler than prejudice, bias names any tendency or lean, conscious or not, from a harmless taste for garden tomatoes to a pattern that quietly costs someone playing time. Only when a lean hardens into judgment made in advance — usually about people — has it crossed into prejudice.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

prejudice: Prejudice is a lean that has hardened into judgment made in advance, usually about people, and it resists evidence. Bias is the broader, often gentler word: any tendency or tilt, conscious or not, harmless or costly. Every prejudice is a bias, but a bias for garden tomatoes is no prejudice.

slant: A slant is a deliberate tilt in how a story gets told — the writer chooses which facts to stress. A bias needs no chooser at all: it can sit in a habit or a system, unnoticed by everyone. A slant is aimed; a bias may simply be there.

partiality: Partiality is favoritism from someone who ought to be neutral — a referee, a judge, a teacher grading papers. Bias is wider: any lean at all, in anyone, with no duty of neutrality required. A grandfather's bias toward his own tomatoes wrongs no one; a referee's partiality does.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

impartiality: the even hand that favors neither side

objectivity: judgment ruled by the facts alone

Where it sits · how hardened and hostile the tilt grows — leaning → bias → bigotry

leaning vs. bias: A leaning is gentler than a bias — a slight tilt of taste you can set aside the moment it matters.

bigotry vs. bias: Bigotry goes far beyond bias: a bias may be an unnoticed lean, while bigotry is the lean hardened into fixed, hostile contempt.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bias

Root — bias: a slant, an oblique line (French biais; deeper origin uncertain)

Put it together

Put it together: Bias came into English from French biais, 'a slant, an oblique line,' and its deeper origin is uncertain. Lawn bowlers still use the oldest English sense: a bowl's bias is the built-in weighting that makes it curve as it rolls — exactly the picture of a mind with a built-in lean. There is nothing to peel off: the word arrived whole.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Bias slipped into English from French biais, 'a slant,' a word whose own ancestry is uncertain — perhaps Greek, perhaps not. It never built an English word family: bowlers kept the rolling-curve sense, tailors cut cloth 'on the bias,' and the mind's lean took over from there. No prefix, no suffix, no cousins to find.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral

Bias is the everyday, often gentle word for a lean — you can admit a bias with a smile. Prefer prejudice when the lean has hardened into pre-made judgment about people, and partiality for favoritism by someone who ought to be neutral, like a referee or a judge.
